**Answer: t = q^h + 1**

**Setup.** Write N = |X|. A given (h−1)-subspace (vector dimension h) lies in (q^{(k−1)h} − 1)/(q − 1) hyperplanes of PG(kh−1, q). Double counting incidences between X and hyperplanes gives

N · (q^{(k−1)h} − 1)/(q − 1) ≤ t · (q^{kh} − 1)/(q − 1).

For k = 4 this gives N ≤ t(q^{4h} − 1)/(q^{3h} − 1). The stated bound (t − 2)q^h + t is a sharper, Griesmer-type bound, and I am taking it as given.

**Check at h = 1.** Here X is a set of points in PG(3, q) with at most t points on any plane, and N = (t − 2)q + t. Setting t = q + 1 gives N = q² + 1. That is exactly the size of an ovoid, which meets every plane in 1 or q + 1 points. For q > 2 the Barlotti–Panella-type classification says such sets are ovoids, so the only admissible t is q + 1.

**Extension to general h.** The natural generalization of this extremal case is t = q^h + 1. Substituting gives N = (q^h − 1)q^h + q^h + 1 = q^{2h} + 1, the analogue of an ovoid for (h−1)-subspaces. I did not derive this value from the paper's proof; it is the value that matches the h = 1 case and the size q^{2h} + 1.

ANSWER: q^h + 1
